analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling and uses the revenue to fund retired coal miners' health benefits.
analysis.headline: The House set up floor debate on the bill but never gave it a final vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005; the bill had no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a leasing program for oil and gas on the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, repealing the 1980 law that bars drilling there. It would cut the fees coal companies pay into the abandoned mine clean-up fund, and it would route a share of the new Arctic oil revenue into a fund paying retired coal miners' health benefits, so the benefit promises are financed by drilling rather than by general tax money. It would also waive or cap some of the health-premium liability that coal operators currently owe for retired miners.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil companies gain access to a long-protected Arctic refuge, with a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres required within 22 months and a guaranteed royalty of at least 12.5% for the public. Coal operators gain three ways: the abandoned-mine reclamation fee they pay per ton is cut, certain operators' back premiums to the miners' health fund are refunded or waived, and they can buy their way out of future premium liability with a prepayment. Retired union coal miners and their widows gain a dedicated stream of money — Arctic oil revenue — pledged to keep their health benefits funded.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, coal operators, retired miners

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Department to open the Arctic coastal plain to competitive oil and gas leasing, with a first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months of enactment, and repeals the statutory ban on producing oil and gas from the Arctic Refuge.

Creates a 'Coal Mining Fairness Fund' financed by the Arctic coastal plain's bonus, rent, and royalty revenue, and uses it to pay the premiums that fund retired coal miners' health benefits, including refunds to operators of premiums paid in fiscal 2004.
Cuts the abandoned-mine reclamation fee paid by coal operators, and repeals the use of reclamation-fund money for rural lands reclamation and for outside research and technical-assistance contracts.

Waives the health-fund premium owed by coal operators to the extent it is paid out of the new fund, lets operators prepay their way out of future premium liability, and limits the liability that can reach related companies or successors.
Sends 50% of the Arctic leasing revenue to the State of Alaska and directs leaseholders to hire Alaska Natives and Native corporations for a fair share of employment and contracting.

analysis.who_pays: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain — about 1.5 million acres — loses its statutory protection against oil development, with the bill deeming drilling 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose, relying on a 1987 environmental review, restricting analysis to a preferred action and one alternative, and limiting court challenges to the D.C. federal appeals court. Communities and states with abandoned coal mines lose reclamation funding as the per-ton fee is cut and rural-lands reclamation and research uses are repealed. The general Treasury gives up a stream of mineral revenue that would otherwise flow to it, and taxpayers stand behind repayable advances to the miners' fund that must be repaid by 2009.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Arctic Refuge and mine-scarred communities

drawbacks.text: The bill declares drilling 'compatible' with the purposes of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, deems a 1987 environmental review sufficient, requires analysis of only the preferred leasing action and one alternative, gives the public only 20 days to comment, and limits judicial review to the D.C. federal appeals court with the agency's choice presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence — a set of shortcuts that makes the 'environmentally sound' standard hard to enforce.

Cutting the reclamation fee from 35 to 28 cents (with parallel cuts in the lower tiers) and repealing rural-lands reclamation and research uses leaves less money to clean up abandoned coal mines, including the acid mine drainage that pollutes water in coal states.

The miners' health benefits become dependent on a fund fed by Arctic oil revenue, with advances that must be repaid with interest by September 30, 2009 — so if drilling revenue disappoints, the benefit stream is at risk.

Waiving and capping operators' premium liability, including a new safe harbor for successors that buy assets at fair market value, shifts legacy coal health costs away from companies and onto the new federally financed fund, weakening the companies' own responsibility for workers they employed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promise to retired coal miners — people owed health benefits after a lifetime in the mines — is genuine, and tying it to oil revenue rather than new taxes was the bill's political selling point. But the trade is steep: the money exists only if a protected wildlife refuge is opened to drilling, the deal simultaneously cuts the fees companies pay to clean up old mines and reduces the liability coal operators owe for their former workers, and the environmental review and court-access provisions are written to make the drilling program hard to challenge. The miners' piece is real; the rest is a transfer to two extractive industries dressed as a miner-benefit bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed a rule to debate the bill, but no final vote was ever taken, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Representative Richard Pombo of California introduced the bill on June 9, 2004, combining an Arctic Refuge oil leasing program with changes to the abandoned mine reclamation fund and retired miners' health benefits; it had no cosponsors.

It was referred to the House Resources Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, but neither committee produced it — instead the Rules Committee reported a resolution providing for one hour of debate on the bill alongside a companion measure, H.R. 4513.

The House adopted that rule on June 15, 2004, setting up floor consideration, but the record shows no further action: no floor debate transcript entry, no amendment votes, and no up-or-down vote on the bill itself.
The bill expired with the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005, having never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge stayed closed to drilling, and coal operators kept paying full reclamation fees and health-fund premiums — the industries the bill would have helped gained nothing. Retired miners also gained nothing, since the promised health-benefit funding died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arctic Refuge protection; oil and coal industries gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a roll call, so there is no vote record to split by party; it was a Republican-sponsored effort with zero cosponsors of either party, advanced by a rule the Republican majority passed on June 15, 2004.

industries.note: The bill opens a protected wildlife refuge to competitive leasing with a mandated first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months, guaranteeing industry access it has sought for decades, at a public royalty of at least 12.5%. The public gets revenue but loses the refuge's statutory protection, and the bill's environmental-review shortcuts make the promised protections hard to enforce in court.

The bill cuts the abandoned-mine reclamation fee coal operators pay per ton, refunds or waives certain operators' back premiums to the retired miners' health fund, allows prepayment to escape future premium liability, and narrows how liability can reach related companies and successors. Their costs shrink, while the abandoned-mine clean-up fund that protects mine-scarred communities is depleted.

industries.industry: Retired union coal miners and their widows
industries.note: A dedicated fund fed by Arctic oil revenue would pay the premiums keeping retired miners' health benefits alive, and the abandoned-mine fund would be directed toward their benefit plans. It is the one provision that serves ordinary people directly, but it depends entirely on drilling going forward.

industries.industry: States and tribes with abandoned coal mines
industries.note: Repealing the rural-lands reclamation and research uses of the fund, and cutting the fee that fills it, means less money to reclaim dangerous abandoned mine lands and treat acid mine drainage in coal-producing states.
